components.gap: Durrett (p. 53, PDF p. 61) defines (S,S) to be nice when there is a 1-1 map phi from S into R with phi and phi^{-1} both measurable, remarks that such spaces are often called standard Borel spaces, and asserts that for this class the generalization of Kolmogorov's theorem is trivial. The handbook (lines 174-181) defines instead a Borel real coding (a measurable isomorphism onto a Borel subset of R) and says only that the source calls the class nice. Durrett's own definition, which imposes no Borel-image condition, is not stated, and the relation between nice spaces and Borel real codings is neither stated nor proved on the route; later chapters translate the source's nice-space hypotheses into the Borel-coding one.

components.gap: Durrett (p. 53, PDF p. 61) states that Theorem 2.1.21 is not valid for arbitrary measurable spaces, attributing the first example (an infinite product of different spaces) to Andersen and Jessen (1948), with references to Halmos (1950) p. 214 and Neveu (1965) p. 84, and citing Wegner (1973) for an example with all factor spaces equal; he then asserts that for nice spaces the generalization is trivial. The handbook only declines to infer an extension for arbitrary measurable spaces (lines 276-277) and proves the generalization for Borel real codings. The source's failure claim, its attributions and references, and the relation of his nice-space assertion to the Borel-coding hypothesis (see C009) are absent from the route.

components.gap: Durrett's 'Caveat emptor' (p. 54, PDF p. 62) says the proof of Theorem 2.1.22 is light on details, refers to Section 13.1 of Dudley (1989) for a fuller treatment, and draws the consequence that for Borel subsets of a complete separable metric space the continuum hypothesis holds: each such set is finite, countably infinite or of the cardinality of the reals. The boundary (lines 297-299) alludes to 'the subsequent source discussion of the cardinality of uncountable Borel sets' but neither states the claim, nor its attribution to Dudley, nor supplies or locates its proof on the route.
